doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

title: Fania, salsa and combining Latin and soul
summary: The salsa marketing label, why he kept Latin and soul separate, and 'Watermelon Man' as an example.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: When you were with Fania Records, did they have, I’m reading a quote here. I think it may have come from your website, but I’m going to read it. It said, “The name salsa literally meaning sauce, has been in use since the late 1960s, popularized by New York’s
Fania Records as a catchy marketing label. Salsa is often thought of as a Latin essence as the word soul has been a description for black American essence.”
Very good. Whoever wrote that hit the nail on the head.

So combining Latin and soul music, I’m trying to form a question about how deliberate, as an arranger, you’re thinking here’s the Latin, all these Latin grooves, and over here we’ve got this soul feel and you’re sitting writing a chart, how do you grab that? How do you combine Latin and soul?

Well generally as I recall they were two different things. When I wrote a Latin arrangement I was thinking strictly Latin, using jazz harmonies in some places to spice it up, but not thinking about soul music. There were some bands, like Mongo, there was another fellow named Pucho who also recorded funky kind of things with a Latin rhythm section and in those cases yes, that was thinking in a funky soulful kind of way. But I never, it wasn’t something that I would combine. Each one was sort of like its own — it was important to do it authentically.
I guess Herbie Hancock’s vamp on “Watermelon Man” is a good example of it.
